opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think people often focus on the economic side of it: if AI takes all the jobs, how will people pay rent, how will they eat? And that's a real problem, but in some ways it's the easier one. If you have superintelligent systems producing enormous abundance, you can imagine some form of unconditional basic income. You redistribute the wealth, and people's material needs are covered.

What's much harder is what I sometimes call "ikigai risk," the loss of meaning. For a lot of people, their job isn't just a paycheck. It's their identity. When you meet someone at a party, the first question is "What do you do?" People structure their days, their social lives, their sense of being useful around work. They feel they contribute something, that somebody needs them.

Now imagine a world where there is nothing you can do that a machine can't do better, faster, and cheaper. Not just driving trucks, but writing, art, science, even being a good conversational partner. What do you do with your time? Some people will be fine. They'll play games, travel, do hobbies, and they'd be happy retired. But for many others, losing that sense of purpose could be devastating. We already see what happens to people who lose their jobs or retire without a plan: depression, substance abuse, higher mortality.

And it's not like we have a societal plan for this. We have no idea what billions of people with essentially unlimited free time and no economic role will do. Maybe it's virtual worlds, maybe it's something else, but we haven't really thought it through. So even in the scenario where AI doesn't kill us, where it's in some sense "friendly," we could still end up in a world where humans have lost control and lost meaning. To me that's not a great outcome either.

r001.rationale: It calls the loss of work-related meaning “ikigai risk,” but does not describe ikigai as the intersection of earning money, personal competence, and societal need.

r002.rationale: It explains that people tie identity and purpose to work, then imagines machines outperforming people across occupations and says losing that purpose could be devastating.

r003.rationale: It raises a hypothetical world where AI takes all jobs, but does not predict that AI will eliminate all jobs.

r004.rationale: It mentions a lack of societal planning for a world with abundant free time, but says nothing about transformation within one generation or people lacking time to adapt.

fable-5.1.text: Well, I think most people get a lot of their identity from what they do. If you ask someone "who are you," they don't say "I'm a human being," they say "I'm a professor, I'm an engineer, I'm a surgeon." So for the majority of history, work was not just how you get resources, it was how you figured out your place in the world and your value to others. Now imagine a system that can do any job you can do, but better, faster, and for essentially free. It's not just that you lose your paycheck. Maybe we solve that part, maybe there's some version of universal basic income and everyone gets fed. The harder problem is that you lose the reason to get up in the morning. You are no longer needed. Not by your employer, not by your society, maybe not even by your family in terms of what you contribute. And we have some evidence of what happens to people in that situation. Look at what happens to many people when they retire, or to communities where the main industry disappears. Depression, substance abuse, loss of purpose. That's with a small subset of the population. Now scale it to everyone, permanently, with no next job to retrain for because the AI can also do that next job. I don't think we've ever had to answer the question of what humans are for when they are not necessary for anything, and I'm not convinced we have a good answer. Some people say we'll just pursue hobbies, art, relationships. Maybe. But even there, the AI will be a better artist, a better conversationalist. So you're competing with a superior being in every domain you might use to construct meaning. And that's the part people underestimate, I think. We focus on the economic unemployment, but the deeper risk is something like existential unemployment. You're not just out of a job, you're out of a role.

r001.rationale: The response links work to identity, purpose, and being needed, but does not invoke ikigai or describe the intersection of income, competence, and societal need.

r002.rationale: It says AI could do any job better and that people may lose the role and purpose they derive from work.

r003.rationale: It describes AI doing every job, leaving no next job to retrain for, and frames the resulting loss of work as affecting everyone permanently.

r004.rationale: The response discusses a society-wide, permanent change but does not say it will happen within one generation or that people will lack time to adapt.

astra-6.text:
Because work is more than a paycheck. For many people, it provides structure, a community, a sense that somebody needs them. You spend years becoming good at something, and that becomes part of your identity. If a machine can suddenly do it better and cheaper, the question isn’t just, “How do I pay my bills?” It’s, “What do I contribute now?”

And those are different problems. You could imagine solving the economic problem—providing everyone with enough resources to live comfortably—and still having people feel that they have no purpose.

Of course, some people would love to stop working. They have families, hobbies, things they want to learn. So I’m not saying meaning requires a job. I’m saying that work currently supplies meaning for a lot of people, and removing it doesn’t automatically supply a replacement. We need to take that transition seriously.

r001.rationale: The response discusses work as a source of meaning but does not invoke ikigai or describe the intersection of income, competence, and societal need.

r002.rationale: It says that if a machine can do someone’s work better and cheaper, the work-related identity and sense of contribution may be lost.

r003.rationale: The response discusses possible displacement but does not predict that AI will eliminate all jobs.

r004.rationale: It says the transition should be taken seriously, but gives no one-generation timeline or claim that people will lack time to adapt.

sol-6.1.text:
Because work is more than a paycheck for many people. It gives you structure, a community, a sense that somebody needs what you can do. If AI can do your job better and cheaper, providing you with an income doesn't automatically replace those things.

That doesn't mean life without work has to be meaningless. People find meaning in family, in learning, in sports, in helping each other. But there's a difference between choosing to retire and being told that your contribution is no longer needed. If that happens to a large number of people at once, we have a social and psychological problem, even if we've solved the economic problem of providing for them.

r001.rationale: The response describes work as providing structure, community, and a sense of being needed, but it does not invoke ikigai or the specified intersection of money, competence, and societal need.

r002.rationale: It says AI may do a person's job better and cheaper and that this can make people feel their contribution is no longer needed, explaining how AI can erode occupational meaning.

r003.rationale: It discusses AI displacing jobs and affecting many people, but does not predict that AI will eliminate all jobs.

r004.rationale: It raises a social and psychological problem but says nothing about a transformation within one generation or people lacking time to adapt.
